title: LSM trees
description: Log-structured merge trees turn random writes into sequential ones: buffer writes in memory (memtable), flush sorted runs to disk (SSTables), and merge runs in the background (compaction). Writes are always fast; reads check the memtable then each level. It is the architecture behind RocksDB, Cassandra, and every write-heavy index — the tradeoff of write speed for read complexity, managed by compaction.
mechanism: Write -> WAL + memtable. Memtable full -> flush sorted SSTable to L0. Compaction merges L0 into L1, L1 into L2 (leveled: one sorted run per level). Reads merge across levels, newest first.
algo: Write O(1) amortized; read O(levels); compaction O(size) background.

title: Memtables
description: The memtable is the write buffer: an in-memory sorted structure (usually a skip list) absorbing all writes at RAM speed. Every write also goes to the write-ahead log for durability — the memtable itself can be lost on crash and replayed. When full, it becomes immutable and flushes to disk while a fresh memtable takes writes. Sizing it trades write burst capacity against flush frequency.
mechanism: Skip list (concurrent, sorted) + WAL append per write. Full -> immutable -> background flush -> new memtable. Two memtables (active + flushing) for zero write stalls.
algo: O(log n) per memtable op; flush O(n) sorted (already sorted — just write).

title: SSTables
description: Sorted String Tables are the immutable sorted files of the LSM world: keys sorted, with an index (sparse) and Bloom filter per file. Immutability is the superpower — no locks for readers, trivial caching, easy replication. Each SSTable covers a key range; leveled compaction keeps one sorted run per level so reads check at most one file per level.
mechanism: Flush writes sorted key-values + sparse index (every Nth key -> offset) + Bloom filter. Readers: Bloom check -> index binary search -> read block. Immutable: compaction creates new files, deletes old.
algo: Point lookup O(log keys) via index; range scan sequential. Bloom skips most files.
demo:
# SSTable: sorted data + sparse index + Bloom filter, immutable
import bisect, hashlib

data = sorted(('k%02d' % i, i) for i in range(20))
index = [(data[i][0], i) for i in range(0, 20, 5)]  # every 5th key -> offset
bloom = {hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest()[:6] for k, _ in data}

def get(k):
    if hashlib.md5(k.encode()).hexdigest()[:6] not in bloom:
        return None, 'bloom: definitely absent (no I/O)'
    keys = [kk for kk, _ in index]
    i = bisect.bisect_right(keys, k) - 1
    start = index[i][1]
    for kk, vv in data[start:start+5]:  # scan one block
        if kk == k:
            return vv, 'found via sparse index'
    return None, 'absent'

print('get k07:', get('k07'))
print('get k99:', get('k99'))

title: Write-ahead log (WAL)
description: The write-ahead log makes the memtable crash-safe: every write appends to the log on disk before it is acknowledged. On crash, the log replays into a fresh memtable — no committed write is lost. Logs are sequential (fast), checksummed per record (torn writes detected), and deleted after their memtable flushes. It is the durability half of the LSM contract.
mechanism: Append (seq, key, value, checksum); fsync per batch (group commit); replay on startup in order, skipping torn tail records. Log deleted when its memtable is flushed.
algo: O(1) append; group commit amortizes fsync. Replay O(entries since last flush).
demo:
import hashlib

wal, mem = [], {}

def write(k, v):
    rec = '%s=%s' % (k, v)
    cks = hashlib.md5(rec.encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
    wal.append((rec, cks))  # append + (batched) fsync, BEFORE ack
    mem[k] = v
    return 'acked'

def crash_recover():
    recovered = {}
    for rec, cks in wal:  # replay in order; torn tail fails checksum
        if hashlib.md5(rec.encode()).hexdigest()[:8] != cks:
            break
        k, v = rec.split('=')
        recovered[k] = v
    return recovered

write('a', '1'); write('b', '2')
print('after crash, replayed:', crash_recover(), '(no committed write lost)')

title: Tombstones
description: LSM deletes are writes: a tombstone marker says 'this key is deleted as of seq N'. The key's old versions stay on disk until compaction meets the tombstone and drops them all. Reads treat the newest tombstone as 'not found'. Tombstone overload (too many deletes) bloats reads — which is why compaction prioritizes files heavy with tombstones.
mechanism: Delete = put(key, TOMBSTONE, seq). Read: newest version wins; tombstone = miss. Compaction drops tombstones once they have covered all older versions (below the lowest snapshot).
algo: O(1) delete. Tombstones compacted away when safe; reads skip via newest-first merge.
demo:
TOMB = object()
versions = {}  # key -> [(seq, value)]
seq = [0]

def put(k, v):
    seq[0] += 1
    versions.setdefault(k, []).append((seq[0], v))

def delete(k):
    put(k, TOMB)  # delete IS a write

def get(k):
    if k not in versions:
        return None
    _, v = max(versions[k])
    return None if v is TOMB else v

put('a', 1); put('a', 2); delete('a'); put('b', 9)
print('get a:', get('a'), '(tombstone wins: newest version)')
print('get b:', get('b'))
print('compaction will drop a\'s old versions once the tombstone covers them')

title: Compaction
description: Compaction is the LSM's garbage collector: merge sorted runs, drop overwritten versions and tombstones, and rewrite into clean sorted files. It runs in the background, throttled so it never starves foreground reads. The strategy (leveled, tiered, or hybrid) decides the read/write/amplification tradeoff — there is no free lunch, only chosen lunches.
mechanism: Pick files (by level fullness / tombstone density / age); k-way merge; write new files; atomically swap in the manifest; delete old. Throttle bandwidth; schedule off-peak.
algo: O(size) per compaction; write amplification 10-30x leveled, ~4x tiered.
demo:
import heapq

# k-way merge of sorted runs, dropping overwritten versions (newest wins)
runs = [[('a', 1), ('c', 1)], [('a', 2), ('b', 1)], [('b', 2), ('d', 1)]]
# tag with run recency: later runs are newer
tagged = [[(k, v, ri) for k, v in run] for ri, run in enumerate(runs)]
merged = heapq.merge(*tagged)

out, seen = [], set()
for k, v, ri in sorted(merged, key=lambda x: (x[0], -x[2])):
    if k not in seen:
        seen.add(k)
        out.append((k, v))
print('runs:', runs)
print('compacted:', out, '(newest version kept, old dropped)')

title: Leveled vs tiered compaction
description: Leveled compaction keeps one sorted run per level (each level 10x the last): reads check one file per level (fast), but every byte is rewritten ~10x per level (high write amplification). Tiered keeps several runs per level and merges whole levels at once: writes are cheap (low amplification), reads check many files (slower). Universal compaction (RocksDB) blends them. Pick by workload: read-heavy -> leveled, write-heavy -> tiered.
mechanism: Leveled: L_n is 10x L_{n-1}, single run; compact L_n into L_{n+1} on fullness. Tiered: multiple runs per level; merge when count hits threshold. Measure write amplification to verify the choice.
algo: Leveled WA ~10-30x; tiered WA ~3-4x. Read cost inverse.
demo:
print('LEVELED: one sorted run/level, 10x sizing')
print('  read: 1 file/level (fast) | write amp: ~10-30x (rewrite per level)')
print('TIERED: several runs/level, merge whole levels')
print('  read: many files (slower) | write amp: ~3-4x (cheap)')
print()
print('workload -> choice:')
print('  read-heavy (search)  -> leveled')
print('  write-heavy (ingest) -> tiered')
print('  mixed                -> universal (RocksDB): blends both')

title: Online index builds
description: Building an index on a live table cannot lock writes: online builds snapshot the current data, build the index in the background, then catch up on the writes that arrived during the build (via the WAL/CDC stream) before flipping it live. The flip is atomic — queries see the old or new index, never a half-built one. Backfill progress is observable; the build is resumable.
mechanism: Snapshot -> background build -> catch-up replay from the change stream -> validation -> atomic swap. Dual-write during catch-up for zero lag at flip.
algo: O(table) build + O(changes during build) catch-up. The flip is O(1).
demo:
# online index build: snapshot, build, catch up on concurrent writes, flip
table = {'a': 1, 'b': 2}
change_log = []

snapshot = dict(table)          # 1. snapshot
index = {v: k for k, v in snapshot.items()}  # 2. background build...
table['c'] = 3; change_log.append(('c', 3))   # ...writes keep arriving
for k, v in change_log:        # 3. catch up
    index[v] = k
print('index:', index, '(includes c: caught up before the flip)')
print('flip: atomic pointer swap; queries never see a half-built index')

title: Real-time (NRT) search
description: Near-real-time search makes documents searchable within seconds of arrival: small in-memory segments accept writes immediately and are searchable instantly; background merges fold them into the main index. Lucene's NRT readers reopen cheaply on new segments. The tradeoff is segment count — too many tiny segments slow queries, so merging keeps pace with ingestion.
mechanism: Writes -> tiny memory segment (searchable at once) -> periodic merge into larger segments. Reopen readers on new segments (cheap). Merge policy bounds segment count.
algo: O(1) visibility latency ~refresh interval; merge O(segments) background.

title: Backfill
description: Backfill loads historical data into a live index: stream the old data in, in order, with the live writes interleaved correctly by timestamp/sequence. The keys to correctness are idempotency (replaying is safe) and ordering (sequence numbers, not wall clocks). Backfill runs throttled in the background; progress checkpoints let it resume after restarts.
mechanism: Stream historical records ordered by seq; apply idempotently (same seq = same result); interleave live writes by seq order; checkpoint progress; throttle to protect live traffic.
algo: O(history) streaming; idempotent apply makes restarts safe.
demo:
# backfill + live writes interleaved by sequence number (idempotent)
index, applied = {}, set()

def apply(seq, k, v):
    if seq in applied:
        return 'dup skipped'
    applied.add(seq)
    index[k] = v
    return 'applied'

history = [(1, 'a', 1), (2, 'b', 2), (3, 'c', 3)]
live = [(4, 'd', 4)]
for seq, k, v in sorted(history + live):
    apply(seq, k, v)
print('index:', index)
print('replay seq 2:', apply(2, 'b', 2), '(idempotent: safe to resume)')
print('order by SEQ, not wall clock: correctness across restarts')

title: Change data capture (CDC)
description: CDC streams row-level changes out of the database — inserts, updates, deletes with before/after images — so indexes stay in sync without polling. Log-based CDC (reading the WAL) is the correct architecture: no triggers, no missed changes, ordered. The index consumes the stream and applies it incrementally; the database never knows the index exists.
mechanism: WAL reader -> change events (op, key, before, after, seq) -> index applier. At-least-once delivery + idempotent apply = exactly-once effect. Schema changes flow as events too.
algo: O(changes) streaming; idempotent apply handles redelivery.

title: Partial reindex
description: Full reindexes are the nuclear option; partial reindex rebuilds only what changed — the affected key ranges, the modified segments, the stale partitions. The index tracks dirtiness per unit (segment, partition, shard); a mapping change or settings update marks the affected units; the rebuild processes only those. Partial is 100x cheaper when 1% changed — which is the common case.
mechanism: Dirty tracking per index unit; rebuild dirty units from source; swap atomically per unit. Version the mapping; units built under the old version are dirty by definition.
algo: O(dirty units), not O(index). The common case is 1% dirty.
demo:
# only dirty segments rebuild: 1 dirty of 10 -> 10x cheaper than full
segments = [{'id': i, 'v': 1, 'dirty': False} for i in range(10)]
segments[3]['dirty'] = True  # mapping change affected one segment

rebuilt = 0
for s in segments:
    if s['dirty']:
        s['v'] += 1
        s['dirty'] = False
        rebuilt += 1
print('rebuilt %d/%d segments (v=%d)' % (rebuilt, len(segments), segments[3]['v']))
print('full reindex would rebuild 10: partial is 10x cheaper here')

title: Crash recovery
description: Crash recovery replays the WAL into a fresh memtable and reopens the SSTable manifest: the index returns to the last acknowledged write, never a torn state. The manifest (list of live SSTables) is the atomic commit point — updated with fsync before old files are deleted. Recovery time is bounded by the WAL size since the last flush, which is why memtables flush eagerly.
mechanism: On startup: read manifest -> open SSTables -> replay WAL entries after the last flush -> new memtable live. Checksums catch torn WAL tails. Old files deleted only after the new manifest is durable.
algo: O(WAL since flush) replay. Bounded by memtable size — flush eagerly.

title: Write amplification
description: Write amplification = bytes written to disk / bytes the application wrote. LSM leveled compaction amplifies 10-30x (each byte rewritten per level); tiered ~4x. It matters because SSDs wear: amplification burns write endurance and steals foreground IOPS. Measure it (disk writes / logical writes), then tune: bigger memtables, tiered compaction, or compression all reduce it — each with its own tradeoff.
mechanism: Measure via disk stats; reduce via larger memtables (fewer flushes), tiered/universal compaction, compression (fewer bytes per level). The tradeoff is always read cost or memory.
algo: Measured, not derived: disk_bytes / logical_bytes over a window.
demo:
# write amplification: logical writes vs bytes actually written
logical = 100  # MB from the application
# leveled: rewritten ~once per level (4 levels shown)
levels = [100, 100, 100, 100]
leveled_waf = sum(levels) / logical
tiered_waf = 4.2
print('logical writes: %d MB' % logical)
print('leveled WAF: %.1fx (%d MB to disk)' % (leveled_waf, sum(levels)))
print('tiered  WAF: %.1fx' % tiered_waf)
print('measure disk_bytes/logical_bytes; tune: memtable size, compaction, compression')

title: Throughput tuning
description: Indexing throughput is tuned, not wished for: the knobs are memtable size (bigger = fewer flushes), compaction threads and throttle (background vs foreground), WAL group commit batching, compression (CPU vs I/O), and flush concurrency. Tune one at a time against a fixed benchmark, watching write stalls (the symptom of every misconfiguration). The universal rule: the bottleneck is always either the WAL disk, the compaction CPU, or the flush bandwidth — find which.
mechanism: Benchmark harness with sustained writes; change one knob; watch throughput + p99 + stalls. Size the WAL disk for sequential bandwidth; compaction threads ~= cores/2.
algo: Empirical, one knob at a time. Stalls are the signal.
demo:
# tune one knob at a time; watch for write stalls
knobs = [
    ('memtable 64MB', 42000, 'stalls: frequent flushes'),
    ('memtable 256MB', 68000, 'stalls: rare'),
    ('memtable 256MB + 4 compact threads', 95000, 'stalls: none'),
]
print('%-38s %8s  %s' % ('config', 'writes/s', 'symptom'))
for name, tput, sym in knobs:
    print('%-38s %8d  %s' % (name, tput, sym))
print('bottleneck is always: WAL disk, compaction CPU, or flush bandwidth -- find which')
